title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg made with butter

content.title: About
content.content: An omelet or scrambled egg cooked in butter is a simple dish of beaten eggs gently fried in butter, which imparts a rich, creamy flavor. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, vitamin D, and essential minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Domesticated eggs have been used for over 7,000 years, originating in Southeast Asia.
Butter is about 80 % saturated fat but also supplies vitamins A, D, E, and K2.
The "scrambled" technique became popular in Europe in the 19th century as a quick way to cook eggs without a crust.
Slow cooking on low heat keeps the texture soft and preserves more nutrients.
In many cuisines the omelet is finished with herbs, cheese, or vegetables for added flavor.

items.title: Complete protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them an excellent source of high‑quality protein for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The yolk provides B12, riboflavin (B2) and pantothenic acid (B5), which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Eggs are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Choline in the yolk is essential for brain function and lipid metabolism.

items.title: Butter’s fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter supplies vitamins A, D, E and K2, which contribute to vision, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Butter is rich in saturated fats; excessive intake can raise LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with hyperlipidemia should monitor egg consumption.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; cook until the whites are fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet or scrambled eggs hot, garnished with fresh herbs, cheese, tomatoes or avocado. They work as a standalone breakfast, a sandwich filling, a wrap component, or a side to vegetable dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw eggs refrigerated at 1‑4 °C in their original carton. Cooked omelet should be eaten within 2‑3 hours at room temperature or stored in the fridge for up to 24 hours in an airtight container.
